title: The Model T and the Moving Assembly Line
summary: In 1908 Ford's company built a tough, simple car called the Model T, nicknamed the Tin Lizzie. Then Ford's engineers made the cars move past the workers on a long line, so a car could be put together in about an hour and a half instead of half a day. Prices fell so low that millions of ordinary families could finally buy a car.

sections.heading: A Car for the Great Multitude
paragraphs: At the end of the last part, Henry Ford made a big promise: to build a motor car for the great multitude. In 1908 that sounded almost silly. Cars were toys for rich people. They broke down often, many cost more than an ordinary worker earned in two or three years, and you usually needed a paid driver who was also a mechanic. Most Americans still lived on farms or in small towns, connected by dirt roads that turned into mud every spring.

On 1 October 1908 the Ford Motor Company introduced the car that was supposed to change all that. It was called the Model T. The name simply meant that it came after a long list of earlier Ford models with letters such as A, B, C, F, K, N, R and S. The first production cars were built at Ford's brick factory on Piquette Avenue in Detroit, and orders flooded in. Within days of the announcement, Ford had thousands of orders, so many that the company could not keep up.

The Model T was not the work of Henry Ford alone. He described what he wanted, but the detailed design came from a small team working in a locked room at the Piquette plant. Childe Harold Wills was a skilled engineer and metal expert. Joseph Galamb and Eugene Farkas were young engineers who had moved to America from Hungary. Galamb drew much of the car, and Farkas worked on parts such as the axles and frame. Together they turned Ford's wishes into thousands of exact drawings.

What did Ford want? First, the car had to be simple. Anyone with a wrench and a bit of common sense should be able to fix it. Second, it had to be tough enough for terrible country roads. Third, it had to be light, because a lighter car needs a smaller engine and less fuel. And fourth, it had to be cheap to build, which meant using the same design year after year instead of changing it all the time.

The result looked tall and a little awkward, like a carriage on stilts. That was on purpose. The Model T sat high off the ground, so it could roll over ruts, rocks and tree roots that would scrape the bottom of a lower car. Its springs were arranged so that the wheels could twist and bounce over bumps while the body stayed fairly level. Farmers loved that. A car that got stuck in the first muddy field was no use to them.

Under the hood was a four-cylinder engine of about 2.9 litres that made about 20 horsepower. That may not sound like much today, when ordinary family cars often have more than 100 horsepower, but the Model T was light, so 20 horsepower was enough. Its top speed was roughly 65 to 70 km/h (about 40 to 45 mph), which was plenty on roads full of potholes, horses and chickens.

One secret ingredient was a special metal: vanadium steel. Ordinary steel of the time could be brittle, and a broken axle in the middle of nowhere was a disaster. Adding a small amount of the element vanadium made steel much stronger and tougher, so parts could be thinner and lighter without snapping. Ford's team used vanadium steel for important parts such as the front axle. Ford liked to tell a story about examining a French racing car wreck and finding a strong vanadium part in it; whether or not every detail of that story is exact, the metal really did help make the Model T both light and strong.

People soon gave the car nicknames. The most famous was the Tin Lizzie. Nobody is completely sure where it came from. Some say Lizzie was a common, friendly name for a hard-working horse or helper, and the car was the farmer's new dependable workhorse. Whatever its origin, the name stuck, and the Model T was also called the flivver, a slang word for a cheap little car.

sections.heading: Driving a Tin Lizzie: Pedals, Levers and a Crank
paragraphs: If you climbed into a Model T today, you might be very confused. There is a steering wheel, yes, but the rest of the controls look nothing like a modern car. Learning them was part of the adventure for millions of first-time drivers.

On the floor were three pedals. The left pedal controlled the two forward gears: pushed all the way down, it put the car in low gear for starting and climbing hills; let all the way up, it put the car in high gear for cruising. The middle pedal was for reverse. The right pedal was the brake, which worked on the transmission rather than directly on the front wheels. A tall hand lever beside the driver worked as a parking brake and also helped hold the car in neutral.

The speed was not controlled by a pedal at all. Instead there were two small levers just under the steering wheel. One was the throttle, which let more fuel and air into the engine. The other adjusted the timing of the spark, meaning exactly when the spark plugs fired. Drivers had to learn to move the spark lever to the right place before starting, or the engine could kick back.

That kick was the most dangerous part of driving an early Model T. Most early cars were started with a hand crank: a metal handle that stuck out at the front. You turned it to spin the engine until it caught and started running. If the spark was set wrong, the engine could fire too early and whip the crank backward, sometimes hard enough to break a thumb or a wrist. Drivers learned to hold the crank in a special way, with the thumb on the same side as the fingers, to stay safe. As Part 7 told, Charles Kettering's electric self-starter appeared on the 1912 Cadillac. Ford was slower to add one, and an electric starter became available on the Model T from about 1919.

The gearbox itself was clever. It used a planetary gear system, in which small gears circle around a central gear like planets around the Sun. Bands tightened around drums inside the gearbox to select low gear, high gear or reverse. Ford advertised it as a three-speed system, but since one of those speeds was reverse, people today usually describe it as having two forward speeds. Because there was no tricky gear lever to move, many people found it easier to learn than other cars of the time.

The Model T also had a small trick for its electrics. Instead of a separate battery and generator in early versions, it used a flywheel magneto: a ring of magnets spinning with the engine's flywheel that produced electricity for the spark plugs and, from about 1915, for the electric headlights too (the earliest cars used gas lamps). The faster the engine ran, the brighter the lights could glow, which meant headlights dimmed when you slowed down. Remember the magneto, because it plays a starring role in the story of the assembly line.

Repairs were part of everyday life. Because the same design was built in such huge numbers, spare parts were cheap and easy to find. Hardware stores and mail-order catalogues sold Model T parts and add-ons, from extra seats to tools. Owners swapped tips, jokes and repair tricks. The car became a kind of shared hobby for an entire country.

sections.heading: Borrowed Ideas: Guns, Pigs and Stopwatches
paragraphs: The Model T was a good design. But a good design alone does not make a car cheap. In its early years, Ford built the Model T much like other carmakers built their cars: the car stayed in one spot while groups of workers walked around it, fetching parts and fitting them on. To build hundreds of thousands of cars, Ford's team would need a whole new way of working. They did not invent it out of nothing. They borrowed ideas from many places and put them together in a new way.

The first big idea was interchangeable parts. In the past, skilled craftsmen made each part slightly differently, then filed and fitted the pieces by hand so they matched. In the early 1800s, United States government armouries such as Springfield in Massachusetts and Harpers Ferry in Virginia worked for decades to make gun parts so exact that any trigger would fit any gun of the same model. They used special measuring tools called gauges and holding frames called jigs and fixtures. This became known as the American system of manufacturing. Ford's factory relied on it completely: if every part was exactly the same, workers did not need to fiddle and file, they just bolted things together.

Making exact parts quickly required powerful machine tools. Ford's factories eventually used tens of thousands of them, including drills with many spindles that could bore all the holes on one side of an engine block in a single operation, and milling machines that could shape a whole row of engine blocks at once. The machines were arranged in the order the work was done, rather than grouped by type, so parts flowed from one machine to the next.

The second big idea came from a surprising place: slaughterhouses. In Chicago meatpacking plants, from the 1860s onward, animal carcasses hung from hooks on overhead rails and moved past a row of workers. Each worker made one cut, again and again, as the carcass slid by. This was really a disassembly line, taking things apart instead of putting them together. A Ford worker named William Klann visited a Chicago slaughterhouse belonging to Swift and Company and came back with the thought: what if we did this in reverse, and built cars as they moved past us?

Other industries had also used moving lines and conveyors. Flour mills moved grain with belts and screw conveyors. Breweries and canneries moved bottles and cans. Ransom Olds, as Part 10 told, had already organised his factory so that Curved Dash Oldsmobiles were assembled in a planned order in 1901, though the cars did not yet move on a powered line.

The third idea was careful timing. An engineer named Frederick Winslow Taylor had become famous for studying workers with a stopwatch, breaking each job into tiny steps and finding the quickest way to do each one. This is often called time study, and a related method that studies each body movement is called motion study. Henry Ford later played down Taylor's influence, but Ford's engineers certainly timed jobs, measured movements and rearranged work so that no one wasted a step.

Finally, there were the people. Historians credit a whole group at Ford for the moving assembly line. Peter E. Martin ran production. Charles Sorensen, nicknamed Cast-Iron Charlie because of his work on the foundry and patterns, was his second in command. Clarence Avery planned and timed many of the experiments. C. Harold Wills, Joseph Galamb and others contributed, and William Klann brought the slaughterhouse idea. Henry Ford pushed hard for lower costs and gave his team the freedom to experiment. So the honest answer to who invented the moving assembly line for cars is: a team, building on ideas that had been floating around for a century.

sections.heading: Highland Park: The Line Starts to Move
paragraphs: The Piquette Avenue plant was soon far too small. So Ford built a gigantic new factory in Highland Park, a town surrounded by the city of Detroit. It was designed by the architect Albert Kahn and opened in 1910. Its walls were filled with so many large windows that people nicknamed it the Crystal Palace. All that glass let daylight pour onto the factory floor, which mattered in an age of dim electric bulbs. The building had several floors, and parts could travel downward through chutes and openings from one level to the next, so gravity did some of the carrying.

Imagine walking onto the Highland Park floor in early 1913. The air smells of hot oil and metal shavings. Leather belts slap and hum overhead, carrying power from spinning shafts to rows of machines. Trolleys rumble past loaded with castings. Even before the moving line, this was one of the most organised factories in the world. By one widely used count, Ford built about 170,000 Model Ts in 1912 (sources differ a little, partly because Ford often counted by business year rather than calendar year). But Ford's engineers believed they could do far better.

Their first real experiment, in the spring of 1913, was with the flywheel magneto, the electricity-making ring of magnets you met earlier. Until then, one skilled worker assembled a whole magneto at a bench, which took about 20 minutes. The engineers split the job into many small steps and lined up the workers along a waist-high rail. Each person did one small task, then slid the magneto along to the next person. Historians who studied Ford's records report that the time per magneto dropped to about 13 minutes, and then, after the rail was raised to a better height and the work was set to move at a steady pace, to about 5 minutes. The same number of people were now making about four times as many magnetos.

That was the moment the idea clicked. If it worked for magnetos, why not for engines, transmissions and axles? Over the next months, Ford's team set up moving lines for one part after another. Then they tackled the biggest challenge of all: the whole chassis, meaning the frame with its axles, springs, wheels, engine and transmission.

Charles Sorensen later wrote that, years earlier, he and a colleague named Charles Lewis had tested the idea one Sunday by dragging a chassis across the old Piquette factory floor with a rope while workers added parts. Historians treat the details as his own account. What is certain is that in 1913 the Highland Park team began pulling chassis along with a rope and a winch, then with a powered chain running along the floor.

On 7 October 1913, the moving chassis line began running. Before the line, building one Model T chassis had taken a team about 12 and a half hours, or roughly 728 minutes. Within a couple of months the time fell to about 2 hours and 40 minutes. By early 1914, after more experiments with the speed of the line, the height of the work and the order of the jobs, the time had dropped to about 93 minutes, roughly an hour and a half. The work was divided into dozens of steps, around 45 by one count, and a finished chassis could roll off the end of the line every few minutes.

The rule of the line was simple: bring the work to the worker, not the worker to the work. Parts arrived by conveyor or slide exactly where they were needed. The worker stayed in one place, did one job, and the moving chassis brought the next one along. Nobody had to walk around looking for bolts.

The results were astonishing. Ford built about 202,000 Model Ts in 1913, about 308,000 in 1914 and about 501,000 in 1915. By around 1914, Ford was by far the biggest carmaker in the world. By 1918, about half of all the cars in the United States were Model Ts. And because the company now built cars so quickly, it could sell them for less, which made even more people buy them, which let the company build even more. Factories everywhere took notice.

sections.heading: Five Dollars a Day
paragraphs: There was a problem. The moving line was fast, but it was also boring and exhausting. Imagine tightening the same few nuts, hundreds of times a day, while the chassis keeps sliding toward you whether you are ready or not. If you were slow, the next worker could not do their job. If you needed a break, someone had to cover for you. Workers complained about the relentless pace, and many simply quit and went to work somewhere else.

In 1913 the turnover, meaning how many workers left and had to be replaced, was enormous. Some departments had to hire around 300 people over a year just to keep 100 jobs filled. Every new worker had to be found, hired and trained, which wasted time and money. A line only works if everyone on it is there and knows what they are doing.

On 5 January 1914, Ford Motor Company made a startling announcement. Its basic pay for qualifying workers would jump from about $2.34 for a nine-hour day to $5 for an eight-hour day. It was more than double what most factory workers in Detroit earned. Ford also moved to three eight-hour shifts, so the factory could run around the clock.

Newspapers around the world reported it. Other business leaders were shocked and some predicted Ford would go broke. Instead, thousands of job-seekers rushed to Highland Park. Reports describe huge crowds standing outside the gates in freezing January weather, hoping to be hired. Turnover fell dramatically, and the company claimed it had dropped from about 32 percent in 1913 to under 2 percent in 1915. The best mechanics in Detroit wanted to work for Ford.

There was also a clever business side to it. Workers earning $5 a day could, after saving for a while, afford to buy the very car they were building. Every lower price and every higher wage widened the circle of people who could own a car. Later, economists used the word Fordism for this combination of mass production, high output and higher wages that let workers become customers.

But the $5 day came with strings attached. Much of the extra money was called profit-sharing, and to get it a worker usually had to have worked at Ford for at least six months and had to live in a way the company approved of. Ford set up what it called the Sociological Department, with dozens of investigators, about 50 according to one account, who visited workers' homes. They checked whether workers drank heavily, gambled, kept their homes clean, saved money, or looked after their children. Workers who did not meet the rules could lose the bonus until they changed. Many immigrant workers were also expected to attend company English classes.

Some families welcomed the help and advice. Others felt it was nosy and controlling: a company had no business telling grown-ups how to live in their own homes. Within a few years the department became smaller and less intrusive, and Ford himself later described that kind of home inspection as out of date.

And the work itself stayed hard. The line set the pace, not the person. Many workers felt like parts of the machine. That tension, between amazing productivity and dull, tiring work, has followed assembly lines ever since, and later factories, as you will see in the next part, tried new ways to give workers more say.

sections.heading: Cheaper Every Year, and Any Color So Long As It Is Black
paragraphs: Ford's plan was to make the Model T a little cheaper almost every year. In 1908 the touring car, the version with seats for about five people, cost about $850. By 1916 the touring car had fallen to about $360. By 1925 the runabout, a two-seater, could be bought new for about $260. Even allowing for changes in the value of money, that was an enormous drop. At the same time, the car got small improvements: electric headlights, an optional electric starter, and later closed bodies with windows that kept out the rain.

By around 1920 Ford was building roughly a million Model Ts a year. Ford factories and assembly plants opened in other countries too, including one at Trafford Park near Manchester in England from 1911, and plants in Canada, Ireland, Denmark and elsewhere. The Model T became a world car.

On farms, the Tin Lizzie became much more than transport. Farmers jacked up a rear wheel and wrapped a belt around it, so the spinning wheel could drive a saw, a water pump, a corn sheller or a washing machine. Companies sold kits that turned a Model T into a small tractor for pulling ploughs. A Model T could carry milk to town, take children to school and bring a doctor to a sick neighbour. Some were turned into trucks, fire engines, snow vehicles with skis, and even little railway cars. Henry Ford also built a real tractor, the Fordson, but for many families the Model T itself was the farm's handiest machine.

Now for the most famous story about the Model T: the color. In his 1922 book My Life and Work, Henry Ford wrote that any customer could have a car painted any colour he wanted, "so long as it is black." This line is often repeated to suggest that every Model T was black. That is not true.

In the early years, from 1908 to about 1913, Model Ts came in several colors, including grey, green, blue and red, depending on the body style and year. Then, from about 1914 to 1925, black really was the only color offered. Why? Because paint takes time to dry, and on a fast assembly line every minute counted. The black enamel Ford used, sometimes called Japan black, dried faster than other colors available at the time, so cars could keep moving. Ford actually used over 30 different kinds of black paint on different parts of the car, each chosen for how it would be applied and dried.

Then, in 1926, colors came back. New quick-drying lacquer paints, such as the Duco lacquer developed by the chemical company DuPont, made bright colors practical on a fast line. Late Model Ts came in shades with names like green, maroon and grey. So the true story is: colors, then black only, then colors again.

sections.heading: The End of the Tin Lizzie
paragraphs: By the mid-1920s the world had changed, and the Model T had not changed nearly enough. Roads were getting better, so people cared less about high ground clearance. Buyers wanted cars that were faster, smoother, more comfortable and better looking. They wanted closed bodies, a normal gear lever, more power, modern brakes and a choice of colors and styles. Many families already owned a car and wanted something newer and nicer, not just another copy of the same old Tin Lizzie.

Other companies were happy to offer exactly that. Some let customers pay in instalments, a little each month, instead of saving up the whole price first. Henry Ford disliked buying on credit and was stubborn about his car. Some of his managers, and reportedly his son Edsel, urged him to design a successor, but for years he refused, until falling sales finally pushed him to approve a new car in 1926. Sales of the Model T began to slide.

Finally, in 1927, Ford gave in. On 26 May 1927, the company celebrated what it called its 15 millionth Model T. Soon afterwards the Model T assembly lines stopped. Including cars built in other countries, more than 15 million Model Ts had been made since 1908, a record for a single car model that would last for about 45 years.

Then Ford's factories went quiet for months while they were retooled, meaning old machines were replaced and new ones set up, for an entirely new car. During that pause, thousands of Ford workers were laid off and Ford dealers had almost nothing new to sell. In December 1927 the new car was unveiled. Ford called it the Model A, starting the alphabet again to show it was a fresh beginning. It had a more powerful engine, a normal three-speed gearbox, four-wheel brakes and a choice of colors. Crowds lined up to see it, and more than four million were built in the following few years.

The Model T had done what Ford promised. It had put the world on wheels. But it had also taught a hard lesson: making the same thing cheaper and cheaper only works while people still want that thing. While Ford's factories stood silent in 1927, a rival company had been quietly gaining ground, by offering buyers something the Model T never did: choice.

deepDive: Historians of technology such as David Hounshell have argued that Ford's achievement was less a single invention than a system. Interchangeable parts had been pursued in American armouries for decades; continuous-flow processing existed in milling, brewing, canning and meatpacking; Olds and others had organised car assembly in sequence. Highland Park combined all of these: highly accurate single-purpose machine tools, a single unchanging product, machines arranged in the order of the work, gravity slides and conveyors, and finally powered lines that set the pace. The numbers show why this mattered. Chassis assembly fell from about 728 labour-minutes to about 93 in roughly six months, and annual output rose from about 170,000 cars in 1912 (by one count) to roughly a million around 1920. Lower costs let Ford cut prices, which expanded demand, which justified even more specialised machines: a feedback loop sometimes described as economies of scale. The costs were real too. Deskilling turned many craft jobs into repetitive tasks, and the extreme turnover of 1913 shows workers voting with their feet. The $5 day is still debated. Some economists describe it as an early example of efficiency wages, where paying above the market rate reduces quitting and absenteeism enough to pay for itself; others stress its paternalism, since the Sociological Department attached moral conditions to the profit-sharing portion. Henry Ford's personal legacy is also complicated: alongside his role in mass production, his newspaper, the Dearborn Independent, published antisemitic articles in the 1920s, for which he later issued a public apology. Finally, the Model T's long life illustrates the danger of over-specialisation. Machines built to make one design extremely efficiently made change slow and expensive, which is why the switch to the Model A required a shutdown lasting months. Later manufacturers, especially Toyota, would look for ways to keep the speed of mass production while making factories more flexible.
funFact: Ford used more than 30 different kinds of black paint on the Model T, each chosen to suit a different part and the way it was painted and dried.

check.q: Why was black the only Model T color from about 1914 to 1925?
check.a: Because black paint dried fastest, keeping the fast assembly line moving
wrong: Because Henry Ford thought every other color was unlucky
Because a law in the United States banned colored cars
Because black cars could drive faster than colored ones
